name: Tenochtitlan
subtitle: The City in the Lake
description: The Mexica island city of Tenochtitlan and its twin Tlatelolco in Lake Texcoco, from the first reed huts of the 1320s to Spanish Mexico City on the eve of the great flood of 1629: the causeways, the dike, the aqueduct from Chapultepec and the canals. Positions are projected from real coordinates; the drawing is an illustration, not a survey.

water.name: Lake Texcoco
water.blurb: A shallow, partly saline lake about 2,240 m above sea level, rich in fish, waterfowl, reeds and edible algae. The Mexica islets were barely above its surface.

water.name: Lake Texcoco
water.blurb: The western bay round the island, called the Lake of Mexico, was kept fresher by springs and, after 1449, by the dike that held back the salt water of eastern Texcoco.

water.name: Lake Texcoco
water.blurb: Crossed by tens of thousands of canoes carrying people, tribute, food, stone and water. The lake rose in the rainy season and the city lived with the risk of floods.

water.name: Lake Texcoco
water.blurb: Shrinking: the western lake was silting into marsh and fields, but the eastern lake still rose against the city in wet years, held back by the dike of San Lázaro.

water.name: Channel between Tenochtitlan and Tlatelolco
water.blurb: The water between the two island cities, narrowing as both built chinampas toward each other. Tlatelolco kept its own ruler and market until 1473.

water.name: Canal of Tlatelolco
water.blurb: The canal along the old boundary between Tenochtitlan and Tlatelolco, crossing the island from lake to lake.

water.name: Acequia de Tezontlale
water.blurb: What was left of the old canal between the city and Tlatelolco, carrying canoes from the eastern lake to the northern barrios. Its western half had been filled in.

water.name: Great canal
water.blurb: The main east-west canal of Tenochtitlan, south of the temple precinct and the ruler's palace, used by canoes bringing goods from the eastern lake.

water.name: Great canal (later the Acequia Real)
water.blurb: The main east-west canal, running past the south side of Moctezuma's palace. Cortés counted canals like this crossed by bridges of long, strong beams that could be raised.

water.name: Acequia Real
water.blurb: The royal canal along the south side of the viceregal palace: Indian canoes unloaded maize, fruit, flowers and firewood at its landings beside the Plaza Mayor.

water.name: Toltec canal (Toltecaacalopan)
water.blurb: A north-south canal on the west side of the city, crossed by the Tlacopan causeway. Its gap was the deadliest of the Noche Triste in 1520.

water.name: Canal to Xochimilco and Chalco
water.blurb: The canal south through the chinampa wards toward the southern lakes, carrying maize, vegetables and flowers into the city.

water.name: Canal de la Viga
water.blurb: The canal from Chalco and Xochimilco: every morning hundreds of canoes brought vegetables, flowers and fodder to the Roldán landing.

water.name: Moyotlan canal
water.blurb: A canal through the south-western ward of Moyotlan, one of many lined with house plots and chinampas.

roads.name: Causeway of Tlacopan
roads.blurb: The western causeway to Tlacopan, the shortest to the mainland, with gaps bridged by removable beams. The aqueduct from Chapultepec ran beside it into the city.

roads.name: Causeway of Iztapalapa
roads.blurb: The great southern causeway, about 7 km long and, Cortés wrote, wide enough for eight horsemen abreast. He entered the city along it on 8 November 1519.

roads.name: Causeway of Coyoacán
roads.blurb: The branch to Coyoacán, joining the Iztapalapa causeway at the fort of Xoloc.

roads.name: Causeway of Tepeyac
roads.blurb: The northern causeway past Tlatelolco to the hill of Tepeyac and its shrine of the goddess Tonantzin.

roads.name: Dike of Nezahualcoyotl
roads.blurb: A dike about 16 km long of stakes, stone and earth, built in 1449 to separate the fresh western lake from the salt eastern lake and protect the city from floods.

roads.name: Calzada de Tacuba
roads.blurb: The old Tlacopan causeway, now a paved road with the aqueduct alongside, lined with houses as far as San Cosme.

roads.name: Calzada de San Antonio Abad
roads.blurb: The old Iztapalapa causeway, the road south to Coyoacán and Iztapalapa past the hermitage of San Antonio Abad.

roads.name: Calzada de Guadalupe
roads.blurb: The old Tepeyac causeway, the pilgrims' road to the shrine of Our Lady of Guadalupe.

roads.name: Calle de San Juan de Letrán
Albarradón de San Lázaro
roads.blurb: The dike built in 1555–56 after a flood, closer to the city than Nezahualcoyotl's, guarding its eastern edge against Lake Texcoco.

bridges.name: Bridge in the Tlacopan causeway
bridges.blurb: One of the gaps in the causeway, spanned by removable beams so that the city could cut itself off.

bridges.name: Bridge over the canal of Tlatelolco
Puente del Palacio over the Acequia Real

districts.name: Sacred Precinct
districts.description: The walled heart of the city and of the Mexica world: the Templo Mayor, temples of other gods, priests' schools, the skull rack, the ballcourt and the warriors' halls. The four quarters of the city met at its gates.

districts.name: Moyotlan
districts.description: The south-western of the four quarters (campan), 'place of mosquitoes', later the Indian parish of San Juan.

districts.name: Teopan (Zoquiapan)
districts.description: The south-eastern quarter, 'place of the god', with Moctezuma's palace on its edge and chinampa wards to the south; later San Pablo.

districts.name: Atzacoalco
districts.description: The north-eastern quarter, facing the eastern lake and the canoe landings from Texcoco; later San Sebastián.

districts.name: Cuepopan
districts.description: The north-western quarter, 'where the flowers open', on the Tlacopan causeway; later Santa María la Redonda.

districts.name: Tlatelolco
districts.description: The twin city on the northern island, founded about 1337, independent until Tenochtitlan's conquest of 1473 and always the home of the great market and the long-distance merchants (pochteca).

districts.name: The traza
districts.description: The Spanish city: a grid of straight streets laid out by Alonso García Bravo in the 1520s round the Plaza Mayor, reserved in principle for Spanish residents.

districts.name: San Juan Tenochtitlan
districts.description: The Indian parcialidad that kept the old name of Tenochtitlan, with its own governor and the market of San Juan.

districts.name: Santiago Tlatelolco
districts.description: The second Indian parcialidad, round the Franciscan church of Santiago and the Colegio de Santa Cruz.

periods.label: Two Island Towns
periods.summary: The Mexica, latecomers to the valley, settle on a marshy islet in Lake Texcoco around 1325; a breakaway group founds Tlatelolco on the next islet north around 1337. Both are tributaries of the Tepanecs of Azcapotzalco. Houses of reed and mud on reclaimed beds, a small earthen temple to Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc, fishing, fowling and trading in reeds.
periods.feel: Wind in the tule reeds, smoke of cooking fires over the water, the splash of poles as canoes push through the shallows.

houses.title: Reed and mud houses
houses.text: Single rooms of wattle and daub or adobe on plots raised from the marsh, thatched with tule reed, grouped round a yard with a granary and a sweat bath. Households of one calpolli (clan ward) lived together round their own small temple.

outskirts.title: New chinampas
outskirts.text: Beds of mud and reed matting staked out into the shallows, the first chinampas, each with a hut, a few willows and maize, beans and chillies growing above the waterline.

periods.label: The Triple Alliance
periods.summary: In 1428 Itzcoatl, with Texcoco and Tlacopan, overthrew Azcapotzalco. Tenochtitlan became an imperial capital: Moctezuma I (1440–69) enlarged the Templo Mayor, built the dike of Nezahualcoyotl after the flood of 1449 and brought fresh water from Chapultepec. Stone and lime replace mud in temples and palaces; in 1473 Tenochtitlan conquered Tlatelolco.
periods.feel: Lime kilns smoking, gangs of tribute labourers hauling stone and stakes, drums from the rising temple.

houses.title: Calpolli patio houses
houses.text: Adobe houses with whitewashed lime plaster and flat roofs, several rooms round a shared patio, one patio per extended family. Each plot fronted a street on one side and a canal on the other, with a canoe tied at the back door.

outskirts.title: Chinampa homesteads
outskirts.text: Long narrow garden beds between canals, edged with willows, each farmed by a household living in a small house at its end. The island grew outward bed by bed.

periods.label: The Island Capital
periods.summary: The capital of an empire of tribute from coast to coast, as Cortés saw it on 8 November 1519: about 13 km² of island laid out on a grid of streets and canals, three causeways to the mainland, the walled Sacred Precinct with the twin-temple pyramid at its heart, palaces of stone and lime, and at Tlatelolco a market that Cortés said drew more than 60,000 people a day.
periods.population: about 200,000 with Tlatelolco (estimates range from 60,000 to 300,000)
periods.feel: Thousands of canoes, conch trumpets at dawn from the temple tops, copal smoke, the market's roar heard a league away.

houses.title: Calpolli patio houses
houses.text: Whitewashed one-storey houses of adobe on stone footings with flat roofs, rooms round a patio, each block reached by a street on one side and a canal on the other. Lords' houses had two storeys, gardens and painted walls.

outskirts.title: Chinampa homesteads
outskirts.text: Long beds of rich lake mud between canals, edged with willows, growing maize, beans, chillies, amaranth and flowers for the city, with the farming family's house and granary at the end of each bed.

periods.label: Viceregal Mexico
periods.summary: Cortés rebuilt the city on the ruins from 1522: a Spanish grid (the traza) round the Plaza Mayor for Spaniards, with Indian barrios round it, San Juan Tenochtitlan and Santiago Tlatelolco. Churches, convents and palaces of grey stone and red tezontle; canals filled in one by one, the lake shrinking, and repeated floods that culminate in the great flood of 1629.
periods.feel: Church bells instead of drums, carriages and mule trains on the causeways, canoes of Indian vendors still crowding the Acequia Real.

houses.title: Spanish casas with patios
houses.text: Houses of stone, tezontle and adobe of one or two storeys, flat-roofed with spouts, built round one or two patios with shops (accesorias) to the street, the richer ones with carved stone portals and balconies.

outskirts.title: Indian barrios and chinampas
outskirts.text: The barrios of San Juan and Santiago Tlatelolco: adobe houses round yards along irregular lanes and canals, chapels for each old calpolli, and chinampas still farmed at the edges.

landmarks.name: Sacred Precinct and the Coatepantli

founding-1350.note: No precinct yet: the shrine stands in an open space among the huts of the first calpolli.

itzcoatl-1440.note: A smaller walled precinct round the enlarged Templo Mayor, with the priests' school and a few temples. Its exact line is not known.

moctezuma-1519.note: A paved square of roughly 300 m a side inside the serpent wall, with four gates toward the causeways and the east; Sahagún lists 78 buildings, temples, schools, altars and priests' houses.

colonial-1620.note: Gone: the cathedral, the archbishop's palace, the Sagrario and the streets of the traza were laid out over it from the 1520s.

landmarks.summary: The walled ceremonial heart of Tenochtitlan, a paved square round the Templo Mayor enclosed by the coatepantli, the 'serpent wall', with gates on the roads to the four quarters.
details: The precinct held the temples of the main gods, the priests' schools and houses, the skull racks, a ballcourt, sacred pools and the platforms of the great sacrifices. Its gates were closed at the massacre of Toxcatl in May 1520. Its extent is reconstructed from excavations under the cathedral and the streets round it; estimates range from about 300 to 500 m a side.

The miniature shows the stucco paving, the wall with its carved serpent heads, the four gates, the priests' houses along the inner side of the wall and a few lesser temples and altars. The main buildings inside are separate models.

landmarks.name: Templo Mayor (Huey Teocalli)

founding-1350.name: The first temple
founding-1350.note: Stages I–II: an earthen platform a few metres high with shrines of wood and thatch to Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc, raised where tradition says the eagle stood on the cactus.

itzcoatl-1440.note: Stages III–IV: Itzcoatl and Moctezuma I enclose the old temple in a larger stone pyramid faced with stucco, with serpent heads and braziers on the platform; the twin stairs face west.

moctezuma-1519.note: Stages VI–VII: perhaps 80–100 m a side at the base and 30–45 m high, twin stairs up to the red shrine of Huitzilopochtli (south) and the blue and white shrine of Tlaloc (north).

colonial-1620.name: Site of the Templo Mayor
colonial-1620.note: Pulled down from 1521 and quarried for the new city; by 1620 houses and streets cover its stump. Its remains were rediscovered in 1978, when electricity workers struck the carved Coyolxauhqui stone.

landmarks.summary: The twin-temple pyramid of Huitzilopochtli, god of war and the sun, and Tlaloc, god of rain, enlarged in seven main stages over the old shrine at the centre of the Mexica world.
details: Each ruler enlarged the temple by building a new pyramid over the old one, so the excavated stump shows seven main stages, from the shrine of the 1320s to the building Cortés climbed in 1519. Its two summit shrines stood for the hill of Coatepec, Huitzilopochtli's birthplace, and the mountain of sustenance of Tlaloc. More than 200 offerings have been excavated since 1978.

The miniature shows stage VII as usually reconstructed: four stuccoed tiers, a double stair with serpent-head balustrades, and the two shrines with their tall roofs. The shrines' roof-crests, the colours and the exact height (estimates run 30–45 m) are reconstruction.
landmarks.function: Main temple of Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc

landmarks.name: Temple of Ehecatl-Quetzalcoatl

itzcoatl-1440.note: Not yet in this form: the round temple excavated behind the cathedral dates from the late 15th century, though an earlier temple of the wind god may have stood here.

moctezuma-1519.note: A round temple on a platform facing the Templo Mayor across the plaza, its stair to the east. Bernal Díaz describes a temple doorway shaped like a serpent's open jaws, probably this one.

colonial-1620.note: Destroyed; colonial houses behind the cathedral stand over it. Remains of its platform were found in 2017 under a hotel on Calle de Guatemala.

landmarks.summary: The round temple of the wind god Ehecatl, an aspect of Quetzalcoatl, whose rounded walls let the wind sweep round it; it stood on the axis of the Templo Mayor.
details: Round temples were built for Ehecatl across central Mexico. The one in Tenochtitlan's precinct sat on a rectangular platform with a semicircular back, in front of the Templo Mayor on the line of the equinox sunrise. Excavations behind the cathedral, announced in 2017, found part of its platform with a ballcourt beside it.

The miniature shows the usual reconstruction: a square-fronted platform with a stair, a circular cella with a conical thatched roof, and a serpent-jaw doorway. Its height and the roof form are interpretation.

landmarks.name: Huey Tzompantli (great skull rack)

itzcoatl-1440.note: An earlier skull rack probably stood here: the excavated platform has several building phases, the earliest perhaps from the mid-15th century.

moctezuma-1519.note: A platform about 35 m long carrying rows of wooden posts strung with the skulls of sacrificed captives, flanked by two towers of skulls set in mortar.

colonial-1620.note: Gone. Its remains were found in 2015 under a house on Calle de Guatemala, behind the cathedral.

landmarks.summary: The great rack of skulls in front of the Templo Mayor, where the heads of sacrificed captives were displayed on wooden poles; the Spaniards were horrified by it.
details: Andrés de Tapia, one of Cortés's captains, described beams with skulls threaded on them and claimed to have counted 136,000, an exaggeration. Excavations from 2015 found the platform and two circular towers of skulls in lime mortar, with skulls of men, women and children, more than 600 so far.
The miniature shows a stuccoed platform with a stair, a grid of posts and crossbars hung with skulls, and the two skull towers. The number of racks and their height are interpretation.
landmarks.function: Display of the skulls of sacrificed captives

landmarks.name: Teotlachco, the ballcourt of the precinct

itzcoatl-1440.note: A ballcourt is likely to have stood in the precinct already; its place in this era is not known.

moctezuma-1519.note: The 'divine ballcourt', an I-shaped court with sloping walls and stone rings, used for ritual games; Sahagún says captives were sacrificed here at the feast of Panquetzaliztli.

colonial-1620.note: Buried. Part of a ballcourt was found in 2017 behind the cathedral, near the temple of Ehecatl and the skull rack.

landmarks.summary: The ritual ballcourt of the Sacred Precinct, where the rubber-ball game was played as an image of the movement of the sun.
details: Players struck a heavy rubber ball with their hips and tried to pass it through stone rings set high in the side walls. Sahagún lists two ballcourts in the precinct. Excavations announced in 2017 found the steps and floor of one behind the cathedral, near the temple of Ehecatl and the Huey Tzompantli, as old sources describe.
The miniature shows the standard Aztec I-shaped court with stuccoed banks and two rings. Its size is estimated from the excavated part.

landmarks.name: Calmecac (school of the priests)

founding-1350.note: Not yet: the first priests lived in huts beside the shrine.

itzcoatl-1440.note: A school for the sons of nobles and future priests, probably already in the north of the precinct; its first form is unknown.

moctezuma-1519.note: Rooms round a patio on a low platform, painted and stuccoed. Remains of a calmecac were found in 2006–2012 under the Cultural Centre of Spain on Calle de Guatemala.

colonial-1620.note: Destroyed; the street of Guatemala and colonial houses cover it.

landmarks.summary: The school where noble boys and future priests learned the calendar, the painted books, songs, history, rhetoric and the strict rule of fasting and self-sacrifice.
details: Each major temple had its calmecac. Pupils slept there, swept the temples, fetched wood, kept vigils and drew blood from their ears and shins as offerings, while learning to read the screenfold books and to speak in the elevated style of the nobility. Commoners' sons went to the telpochcalli of their ward instead.
The miniature shows a stuccoed platform with a ring of rooms round a court, based on the excavated walls and on Sahagún's description. The plan is simplified.

landmarks.name: House of the Eagle Warriors

itzcoatl-1440.note: The building's first phase probably dates from these years; it was rebuilt over it in the late 15th century.

moctezuma-1519.note: An L-shaped hall on a platform north of the Templo Mayor, with a columned porch and benches carved with processions of warriors along its walls.

colonial-1620.note: Buried; excavated in 1981–82, with two life-size clay eagle warriors found by its doorways.

landmarks.summary: A hall north of the Templo Mayor associated with the eagle warriors, the elite order of the army, and with rulers' rites of penance; its carved benches survive.
details: Excavated in 1981–82, the building has rooms with polychrome benches copying those at Tula, braziers with images of Tlaloc, and two ceramic figures of eagle warriors at its entrances. Whether eagle warriors actually met here is debated; it may have been used by rulers for vigils and penance before their accession.
The miniature shows the low platform, stair, pillared porch and stuccoed rooms; the roofs are flat with a small parapet. Upper details are reconstruction.
landmarks.function: Ritual hall, probably of the eagle warriors

landmarks.name: Palace of Moctezuma (the New Houses)

itzcoatl-1440.note: Not yet built. Moctezuma I's palace probably stood west of the precinct; this ground south-east of the temple was houses and gardens.

moctezuma-1519.note: Moctezuma II's palace, begun after 1502: courts, halls of state, council rooms, armouries, storehouses of tribute, apartments for his wives, and gardens, all on a platform beside the main square.

colonial-1620.note: Destroyed in the siege; Cortés built his own houses on its ruins, sold to the Crown in 1562 as the viceregal palace.

landmarks.summary: The palace of Moctezuma II, a city within the city: the seat of government, courts of justice, councils and tribute stores, where, Cortés wrote, some 600 lords attended the ruler every day.
details: Cortés and Bernal Díaz describe a palace of many courts and rooms with walls of stone and lime, cedar ceilings and woven mats, with apartments for the ruler's wives, rooms for visiting lords, a council of war, a tribute office and treasure rooms. The Codex Mendoza draws its plan: the ruler's hall on a raised platform above a courtyard.

The miniature follows the Codex Mendoza plan and Evans's study of Aztec palaces: a stepped platform, a great court entered from the square, the raised throne hall, lesser courts and a garden. Its scale is estimated from the block later occupied by the National Palace.
landmarks.function: Royal palace and seat of government

landmarks.name: Palace of Axayacatl

itzcoatl-1440.note: Not yet built: Axayacatl reigned 1469–81.

moctezuma-1519.note: The palace of Moctezuma's father, west of the precinct. Cortés and his men were lodged here from 8 November 1519 and found the sealed room of Axayacatl's treasure.

colonial-1620.name: Houses of the Marquis of the Valley
colonial-1620.note: Cortés's 'old houses' were built on its site; the Nacional Monte de Piedad stands there today.

landmarks.summary: The palace of the ruler Axayacatl, where Moctezuma lodged Cortés and his men in November 1519 and where the Spaniards were besieged in June 1520.
details: Bernal Díaz says it was large enough to house all the Spaniards and their Tlaxcalan allies (perhaps 2,000 or more), with halls hung with cloth and a temple of its own. The Spaniards held Moctezuma prisoner here, and dug through a freshly plastered wall to find the treasure. After the massacre of Toxcatl the Mexica besieged them here until the flight of the Noche Triste.
The miniature shows a palace of the usual Aztec form: a low platform, a ring of halls round a central court, a smaller inner court and a shrine. Its plan is not known.
landmarks.function: Royal palace; the Spaniards' quarters in 1519–20

landmarks.name: Totocalli, Moctezuma's house of birds

moctezuma-1519.note: Pools of salt and fresh water for waterbirds, galleries with cages of eagles and birds of every colour, and a house of jaguars, pumas, wolves, snakes and dwarfs, kept by 300 men.

colonial-1620.note: Burnt by Cortés during the siege in 1521. The Franciscans built their great convent of San Francisco on or near its site.

landmarks.summary: Moctezuma's aviary and zoo, with pools for waterbirds, cages for birds of prey, and houses of jaguars, pumas and snakes; feathers from its birds supplied the featherworkers.
details: Cortés wrote that ten pools held every kind of waterbird of the land, fed with fish, worms, maize and seeds, while 300 men tended them; another house held birds of prey and animals in cages, fed on turkeys and, Bernal Díaz claims, on the bodies of sacrificed captives. Moulted feathers were collected for featherwork.

The miniature shows a walled garden with pools, an arcaded gallery of cages and pens. Its plan is unknown and the site is debated; this follows the tradition placing it where San Francisco was later built.

landmarks.name: Market of Tlatelolco

founding-1350.note: A small exchange of fish, birds, reeds and lake produce for maize, wood and stone from the mainland, already Tlatelolco's livelihood.

itzcoatl-1440.note: The market grows with Tlatelolco's merchants, who trade far beyond the valley; after 1473 the city is ruled from Tenochtitlan but keeps its market.

moctezuma-1519.note: A plaza ringed by arcades, each kind of goods in its own row, judges keeping order. Cortés claimed more than 60,000 buyers and sellers a day; an anonymous conquistador gave 20,000–25,000, twice that on market days.

colonial-1620.note: Much reduced after the siege; the main markets moved to the Plaza Mayor and San Juan, though a market at Tlatelolco continued.

landmarks.summary: The greatest market of the Americas, which astonished the Spaniards: everything from gold, slaves and cacao to herbs, firewood, cloth and turkeys, sold in ordered rows.
details: Cortés compared it to the square of Salamanca but twice as large; Bernal Díaz said soldiers who had seen Rome and Constantinople had never seen a market so large and well ordered. Goods were sold by count and measure, not weight; cacao beans and cotton cloaks served as money; a court of judges sat in the market and officials patrolled the rows.

The miniature shows the plaza with rows of stalls under cotton awnings, arcades round the edge, the judges' house and a canal landing. The size and layout of the real plaza are estimated; its exact site south-east of the temple is not certain.
landmarks.function: Main market of the Valley of Mexico

landmarks.name: Templo Mayor of Tlatelolco

founding-1350.note: The first temple of the Tlatelolca, a small platform with a shrine, founded around 1337.

itzcoatl-1440.note: Enlarged in stone by Tlatelolco's rulers in rivalry with Tenochtitlan. In 1473 its ruler Moquihuix fell or was thrown from its summit when Axayacatl took the city.

moctezuma-1519.note: A walled precinct with a twin-temple pyramid like Tenochtitlan's, smaller, a round temple and a calendar temple. Cortés and Bernal Díaz climbed the pyramid and saw the whole lake from its top.

colonial-1620.note: Dismantled after the conquest; its stones built the church of Santiago beside it. Its ruins were excavated in the 1960s in the Plaza de las Tres Culturas.

landmarks.summary: The twin-temple pyramid of Tlatelolco beside its great market, rebuilt in rivalry with Tenochtitlan's; the last stronghold of the Mexica in August 1521.
details: Excavations in the Plaza de las Tres Culturas found the pyramid's successive stages, a calendar temple with painted walls, a round temple and burial offerings. From its summit Moctezuma showed Cortés the city, the causeways and the lake 'all full of canoes'. Its stones were reused for the church of Santiago Tlatelolco.

The miniature shows the precinct with its wall, the twin-temple pyramid with a double stair facing west over the plaza, the round temple and the small calendar temple. Heights and shrine roofs are estimated.
landmarks.built: c. 1337; enlarged to the late 15th century

landmarks.name: Fort of Xoloc

itzcoatl-1440.note: Probably not yet built; the causeway here may have had only a bridge.

moctezuma-1519.note: A walled bulwark with two towers where the Coyoacán causeway joins the Iztapalapa causeway, about 2 km south of the precinct. Cortés passed it on 8 November 1519 on his way to meet Moctezuma.

colonial-1620.name: San Antonio Abad
colonial-1620.note: The fort was Cortés's headquarters in the siege of 1521; its site is near the later hermitage of San Antonio Abad on the calzada.

landmarks.summary: A fortified gate on the southern causeway, a stone wall with towers and two gates, guarding the main road into the city from the south.
details: Cortés describes a strong bulwark of stone two estados (about 3.5 m) high with towers and two gates, where the two causeways met. Beyond it, at a bridge where the causeway reached the city (by tradition at Huitzillan), Moctezuma met the Spaniards on 8 November 1519. During the siege of 1521 Cortés took it and made it his camp.
The miniature shows a wall across the causeway with two square towers, a gateway and a timber bridge in front. Its form is interpretation from Cortés's letter.

landmarks.name: Drawbridge of the Toltec canal

moctezuma-1519.note: Where the Tlacopan causeway crossed the Toltec canal on removable beams. On the Noche Triste the Mexica removed the beams and many of the fleeing Spaniards drowned here.

colonial-1620.name: Puente de Alvarado
colonial-1620.note: Remembered as the 'leap of Alvarado', where Pedro de Alvarado is said to have vaulted the gap; the hermitage of the Martyrs, later San Hipólito, was built nearby.

landmarks.summary: A wooden bridge over a canal on the Tlacopan causeway, one of the gaps that the Mexica opened to trap the Spaniards on the night of 30 June 1520.
details: The causeways and streets were cut by canals spanned by beams that could be pulled away. Cortés built a portable bridge for the flight of the Noche Triste, but it jammed at the first gap; at the Toltec canal the gap filled with drowned men, horses and baggage, and the survivors crossed on them.
The miniature shows a canal with stone revetments, a deck of heavy beams that could be lifted out and small guard platforms. Its form is interpretation.

landmarks.name: Aqueduct of Chapultepec

founding-1350.note: Not yet: the Mexica drew water from springs on the islet and from the lake, and carried fresh water from Chapultepec by canoe.

itzcoatl-1440.note: Built under Moctezuma I with Nezahualcoyotl's help, finished in the 1460s: a channel of stone and mortar on an earth dike from the springs of Chapultepec to the city.

moctezuma-1519.note: Two masonry channels side by side on the causeway, one used while the other was cleaned. At the bridges water was sold from canoes.

colonial-1620.name: Aqueducts of Chapultepec and Santa Fe
colonial-1620.note: The Chapultepec channel was repaired; from the 1570s a new arcaded aqueduct brought water from the springs of Santa Fe along the San Cosme and Tacuba roads.

landmarks.summary: The aqueduct that brought spring water from the hill of Chapultepec to the island, about 5 km, running along the Tlacopan causeway into the city.
details: Earlier channels were of clay and reed and broke easily. The masonry aqueduct of the 1460s had a double channel, so one could be cleaned while the other carried water. Cutting it was the Spaniards' first move in the siege of May 1521. In colonial times the city's water came on arches, from Chapultepec and from Santa Fe.

The miniature shows a stretch of the causeway in the lake, with the twin channels on a stone embankment beside the road and a short timber bridge. The 1620 version shows a low arcade. The exact course is reconstruction.

landmarks.name: Dike of Nezahualcoyotl (Albarradón)

founding-1350.note: Not yet built: floods could reach the islets from the salt eastern lake whenever it rose.

itzcoatl-1440.note: Built after the flood of 1449 under the direction of Nezahualcoyotl of Texcoco, with labour from the allied cities: about 16 km of stakes, stone and earth.

moctezuma-1519.note: Kept in repair, with sluices to let canoes through; it kept the lake round the city fresher and its level steadier.

colonial-1620.note: Broken by Cortés's brigantines during the siege and never fully repaired; the dike of San Lázaro (1555–56) was built closer to the city.

landmarks.summary: A dike about 16 km long across Lake Texcoco from Atzacoalco to Iztapalapa, built in 1449 to protect the city from floods and keep the salt water of the eastern lake away.
details: Nezahualcoyotl, ruler of Texcoco and famous as a poet and engineer, designed it for Moctezuma I after a flood. Thousands of workers drove lines of stakes into the lake bed and filled between them with stone and earth. It created the fresher 'Lake of Mexico' round the island in which the chinampas flourished.

The miniature shows a short stretch: a stone-faced embankment between rows of stakes, with a sluice gate and a canoe passage. Its width and height are estimates. The line on the map follows the usual reconstruction.

landmarks.name: Cathedral of Mexico

moctezuma-1519.note: The site lies inside the Sacred Precinct, on the west side of its great plaza, near the temple of Ehecatl and the skull rack.

colonial-1620.note: The small first cathedral (begun c. 1524–32) still in use, while the new cathedral begun in 1573 rises behind it: walls, chapels and the first piers, not yet vaulted.

landmarks.summary: The cathedral of New Spain, first a modest church built with stones of the Aztec temples, then from 1573 the great cathedral that took 240 years to finish.
details: The first church, on the north side of the Plaza Mayor, was small, low and timber-roofed, and was soon judged unworthy of the capital. The new cathedral, planned by Claudio de Arciniega, was begun in 1573 on a raft of piles in the soft lake bed. By 1620 its walls were rising; vaulting began in the following decades, and it was first dedicated in 1656.
The miniature shows the old church with its small tower and, north of it, the unfinished new cathedral: thick walls, buttresses and the stumps of the towers. Heights in 1620 are estimated.

landmarks.name: Viceregal Palace (Palacio Real)

moctezuma-1519.note: The site of Moctezuma's palace, the New Houses.

colonial-1620.note: Cortés's 'new houses', bought by the Crown in 1562: a fortress-like palace of two storeys round several patios, with the audiencia, the royal treasury, the mint and the viceroy's apartments.

landmarks.summary: The palace of the viceroys of New Spain on the east side of the Plaza Mayor, built by Cortés over Moctezuma's palace and later rebuilt as Mexico's National Palace.
details: Cortés rebuilt his houses here with towers and battlements; the Crown bought them in 1562 for the viceroys. Besides the viceroy, it held the high court (audiencia), the treasury, the mint, a prison and barracks. In January 1624 a crowd stormed and burned part of it during the riot against the viceroy Gelves; it burned again in 1692.
The miniature shows the palace as in Gómez de Trasmonte's view of 1628: a long two-storey front with corner towers and battlements, several courts and flat roofs. Details are simplified.
landmarks.function: Residence of the viceroy and seat of government

landmarks.name: Plaza Mayor

moctezuma-1519.name: Square of the palaces
moctezuma-1519.note: The open paved square south of the Sacred Precinct, between the palaces of Moctezuma and Axayacatl, where the Iztapalapa causeway ended.

colonial-1620.note: The main square, crowded with Indian market stalls under mats and awnings, wooden shops (cajones), a fountain, the gallows and the pillory; the stone Parián market came only in 1695–1703.

landmarks.summary: The great square of Spanish Mexico, laid out on the plaza in front of Moctezuma's palace, flanked by the cathedral, the viceroy's palace and the city hall, and filled with a daily market.
details: Spanish writers boasted it was one of the largest squares in the world. Traders sold food, cloth, pottery and flowers; Spanish merchants kept shops under the arcades (portales) on its west and south sides; the city council met in its own building on the south side. In the flood of 1629 it lay under water for years.

The miniature shows the paved square with rows of stalls under mat awnings, a fountain, wooden shops and arcaded fronts on two sides. The arrangement of the stalls is interpretation from views of the 17th century.

landmarks.name: Convent of San Francisco

moctezuma-1519.note: Moctezuma's house of birds probably stood on or near this ground.

colonial-1620.note: The great Franciscan convent: a walled atrium, the church, the open chapel of San José de los Naturales where Indians heard Mass, cloisters, gardens and the school of Pedro de Gante.

landmarks.summary: The mother house of the Franciscans in New Spain, founded in the 1520s by the friars who first evangelized the Mexica, once the largest convent of the city.
details: The 'Twelve' Franciscans arrived in 1524. Their convent grew into a walled precinct with several churches and chapels, cloisters and orchards. In its chapel of San José de los Naturales the Flemish friar Pedro de Gante taught Indian boys reading, music, painting and crafts from the 1520s. Most of it was demolished after 1856.

The miniature shows the walled atrium with corner chapels, the single-nave church with a tower, the open chapel and the cloister. It is simplified from the 17th-century views; the church was rebuilt in 1710–16.

landmarks.name: Santiago Tlatelolco and the Colegio de Santa Cruz

moctezuma-1519.note: The site lay in the temple precinct of Tlatelolco, beside the pyramid.

colonial-1620.note: The Franciscan church of Santiago (rebuilt 1604–10) with its convent, and the Colegio de Santa Cruz (1536), where Nahua students learned Latin and worked with Sahagún on the Florentine Codex.

landmarks.summary: The Franciscan church and college of Tlatelolco, the first European-style school of higher learning in the Americas, built with stones of the Tlatelolco temple.
details: The Colegio de Santa Cruz was founded in 1536 to educate sons of the Nahua nobility in Latin, rhetoric, philosophy and medicine. Its students and teachers produced the Badianus herbal (1552) and worked with Bernardino de Sahagún on the Florentine Codex. By 1620 the college was in decline; the church of Santiago had just been rebuilt in stone.
The miniature shows the fortress-like single-nave church with a tower, the convent cloister and the college buildings round a second court. The college's form is interpretation.

spots.name: Cacao sellers' row
spots.summary: The row where cacao beans, the small change of the Aztec world, were counted out by the hundred and traded for everything else in the market.
details: Cacao came from the hot lands of Soconusco and the Gulf coast. A large cotton cloak (quachtli) was worth 65 to 100 beans depending on its quality; a price list of 1545 values a turkey cock at 200 beans and a large tomato at one. Sahagún warns of counterfeit beans: husks stuffed with earth or wax.

vignettes.text: Sacks of beans from Soconusco are opened on mats. The sellers sort them by size and tip any that sound hollow into a separate basket: the forger's trick is a husk filled with mud.
A woman buys salt and chillies, paying in beans counted from a knotted cloth; for a cloak she will bring the beans in twenties and hundreds, tallied on her fingers.
The rows thin out. Unsold beans go back into the sacks, and a market judge's officer walks past checking measures before the stalls close.

itzcoatl-1440.note: Already the market's currency: Tlatelolco's merchants import cacao from the coasts as trade grows with the alliance's conquests.

spots.name: Obsidian blade-makers
spots.summary: Craftsmen who pressed long razor-sharp blades from cores of obsidian, volcanic glass, while you watched; Spanish friars marvelled at their skill.
details: The black and green glass came from mines at Otumba and Pachuca in the hills north-east of the lake. With a pointed stick braced against the chest, a knapper detached long parallel blades from a prepared core, used for knives, razors and the edges of the wooden warclub (macuahuitl). Barbers shaved with them.

vignettes.text: A knapper sits with a fist-sized core clamped between his feet, leans his weight on a crutch-shaped stick, and a blade as long as a finger springs off with a soft crack.
A warrior's servant buys a row of blades to glue into a new warclub; a barber tests an edge against the hairs of his arm.
The mats glitter with chips. The knapper sweeps the debris into a basket; the tiny flakes will go to make points and scrapers.

spots.name: The market court
spots.summary: A house in the market where judges sat every day to settle disputes and punish cheats, while officials walked the rows checking prices and measures.
details: Cortés reports a 'very fine building' in the market where ten or twelve judges sat, and officers who watched the trading and broke false measures. Sahagún describes the market overseers (tianquizpan tlayacaque) fixing prices. Thieves could be sentenced on the spot; serious crimes were punished by death.

vignettes.text: Two women argue over a measure of maize: the seller's gourd may have a false bottom. An officer carries it in to the judges, sitting on mats at the back of the hall.
A man caught stealing a cloak is brought in. He is a commoner; the judges hear the witnesses briefly and pronounce.
The overseers walk the rows, calling out the day's price of beans and turkeys, as the crowd begins to thin.

itzcoatl-1440.note: Tlatelolco's own judges keep the market until the conquest of 1473; afterwards they answer to Tenochtitlan.

spots.name: Pulque sellers
spots.summary: Sellers of pulque, the milky fermented sap of the maguey, drunk by the old, the sick and at festivals; public drunkenness among the young could be punished by death.
details: Aztec law restricted pulque: elders (traditionally those past 52) could drink, and everyone at certain feasts, but a drunken noble might be executed. Sahagún describes pulque sellers in the market with their jars and gourds. Under Spanish rule the trade was licensed, taxed and boomed, and pulque shops became the taverns of the poor.

vignettes.text: Jars of fresh pulque arrive by canoe from the maguey fields round the lake, the sap gathered yesterday and fermented overnight. It smells sour and yeasty.
An old man with the right to drink sits in the shade with a gourd of it. Younger men walk past without looking: they know the penalty.
The seller pours the dregs back into one jar and covers it with a cloth; pulque spoils in a day.

colonial-1620.name: Pulquería of Tlatelolco
colonial-1620.note: A licensed pulque stall with a shade of mats, crowded on feast days; friars and viceroys repeatedly tried to limit the trade.

spots.name: Featherworkers of Amantla
spots.summary: The ward of the amanteca, the featherworkers, who made shields, headdresses and mosaics of feathers from tropical birds, the most prized art of the Aztecs.
details: The amanteca of Amantla worked for the ruler, the merchants and the market, gluing feathers of quetzal, cotinga, spoonbill and parrot onto paper and cotton backings over stencils. Sahagún devotes a chapter to their methods and gods. After the conquest they made feather mosaics of Christian saints, admired in Europe.

vignettes.text: In a patio the master's wife dyes duck feathers in pots of colour to fill the background; the precious green quetzal plumes are kept in a reed box.
An apprentice cuts each feather to shape with a copper blade and lays it on a paper stencil covered with glue made from orchid bulbs.
A shield with a coyote in blue and green feathers is finished for a war captain; it shimmers as it is turned to the light.

itzcoatl-1440.note: Featherworkers are settled in Tlatelolco's ward of Amantla; the trade in tropical feathers grows with the pochteca's long journeys.

colonial-1620.name: Featherworkers of Santiago Tlatelolco
colonial-1620.note: Feather mosaics of Christ and the saints for churches and for export to Spain, made under Franciscan patronage.

spots.name: A pochteca merchant's house
spots.summary: The house of a long-distance merchant of Tlatelolco, outwardly modest, inwardly rich, from which caravans of porters left for the coasts and Guatemala.
details: The pochteca were a hereditary guild with their own gods, courts and ranks. They travelled for months with porters to trade cloth, obsidian and jewellery for cacao, feathers, jade and jaguar skins, and also spied for the ruler. Sahagún says they hid their wealth, entering the city at night and dressing plainly so as not to provoke the nobles.

vignettes.text: Before dawn a caravan leaves: porters with tumplines and loads of cloth, the merchant with his staff and fan, a priest's blessing still on them.
In a back room the merchant's wife counts bundles of quetzal feathers brought back from the south and wraps them in cotton.
A merchant returns after a year away, slipping in by canoe after dark so that no one sees the size of his cargo.

spots.name: A chinampa farm
spots.summary: A family's long, narrow garden bed built up from lake mud and reed mats between canals, its edges held by willows, giving several harvests a year.
details: Chinampas were made by piling mud and decaying vegetation inside a frame of stakes and planting willows (ahuejote) along the edges. Seedlings were raised in mud seedbeds and transplanted. Calnek found that many house plots inside the city had their own chinampas behind the house. Maize, beans, squash, chillies, tomatoes, amaranth and flowers went to the city by canoe.

vignettes.text: The farmer scoops black mud from the canal bottom with a net on a long pole and spreads it over the bed; it smells of the lake.
His wife cuts the mud seedbed into little cubes, each with a maize seedling, and sets them out in rows along the bed.
A canoe loaded with squash flowers and green chillies is poled off toward the city for tomorrow's market.

itzcoatl-1440.note: New chinampas being staked out into the lake as the city spreads, under the eye of ward officials.

colonial-1620.name: Chinampas of San Pablo
colonial-1620.note: Still farmed by Indian families of the barrio, though the canals silt up and the lake falls; produce goes to the Roldán landing.

spots.name: Canoe landing on the southern canal
spots.summary: A landing where canoes from the southern lakes unloaded maize, firewood, stone and flowers; tens of thousands of canoes worked the lakes.
details: Without wheels or draught animals, everything heavy came by water. A canoe paddled by one man could carry a tonne. Cortés says canoes came and went all day to the city's landings; at the siege he used brigantines against them. The colonial landing of Roldán, on the Canal de la Viga, kept the trade alive into the 19th century.

vignettes.text: In the half-dark the canal is jammed with dugouts; boatmen shout and push off from each other with their poles.
Porters carry bundles of firewood and sacks of maize up the steps to the street, tumplines across their foreheads.
Empty canoes head home south, one with a sleeping boy on a pile of reed mats.

colonial-1620.name: Embarcadero de Roldán
colonial-1620.note: The landing of the Canal de la Viga, where canoes from Chalco and Xochimilco unloaded vegetables, flowers and fodder for the city.

spots.name: Telpochcalli of Moyotlan
spots.summary: The 'house of youth' of a calpolli, where commoner boys in their teens lived, worked and trained for war under veteran warriors.
details: Every ward had its telpochcalli. Boys swept, carried wood and worked on public projects by day, learned to fight and to handle weapons, and at night sang and danced at the house of song (cuicacalli). Their teachers were seasoned warriors; a youth who took captives in battle rose in rank and could leave to marry.

vignettes.text: The boys come back from the lake with bundles of wood for the temple fires, hair cropped short, faces smeared with soot.
In the patio a veteran shows them how to parry with a shield and to strike low with the warclub, to take a captive alive.
Drums from the house of song: the boys dance in lines with the young women until late, under the eyes of the elders.

itzcoatl-1440.note: Each calpolli keeps its own house of youth; the wars of the alliance give the boys their first campaigns.

spots.name: Temple of a calpolli
spots.summary: The small pyramid temple of a calpolli, a ward of related families who shared land, a god, a school and a leader.
details: Tenochtitlan was made up of dozens of calpolli grouped into four quarters. Each had its own temple to its patron god, its telpochcalli and its leaders, who allocated land and organised tribute and military service. After the conquest the friars replaced these temples with chapels, which is why many barrios kept the name of a saint before the old name.

vignettes.text: A priest blows a conch from the little temple platform; the households of the ward stir and the first fires are lit.
Women bring tamales and flowers for the god's feast; the ward's elders sit on the steps discussing the tribute due to the palace.
Copal incense burns in a brazier at the top, a small red light among the flat roofs.

founding-1350.note: A shrine of reed and mud for the calpolli's god, among the first huts on the islet.

itzcoatl-1440.note: Rebuilt on a stone platform as the ward grows rich from tribute and war.

colonial-1620.name: Chapel of San Sebastián Atzacoalco
colonial-1620.note: A Christian chapel serving the old ward of Atzacoalco, with an Indian fiscal and a confraternity in charge of its feasts.

spots.name: A house compound of Cuepopan
spots.summary: An ordinary household compound: several related families in single-storey rooms round a shared patio, with a street door on one side and a canoe at the back.
details: Sixteenth-century land documents studied by Calnek show house plots of several rooms facing a patio, often with a chinampa garden behind. Houses had adobe walls on stone footings, flat roofs and a sweat bath (temazcal). Floors were swept earth or plaster; people slept on mats, cooked on a three-stone hearth and stored maize in a granary.

vignettes.text: The slap of hands shaping tortillas on the griddle; the women have been grinding maize on the metate since before dawn.
The grandmother weaves cotton on a backstrap loom tied to a post in the patio, a toddler asleep on a mat beside her.
The family eats beans, tortillas and chilli sauce by the hearth; a dog barks at a canoe passing in the canal behind.

spots.name: Water-sellers at the aqueduct
spots.summary: Where the aqueduct from Chapultepec reached the city, water-carriers filled jars and canoes to sell fresh water through the streets and canals.
details: The lake water around the city was brackish, so drinking water was precious. Cortés says canoes took water from the aqueduct where it crossed the bridges and sold it through the city, paying the ruler a fee. In colonial Mexico City the aguadores, carrying huge jars on tumplines, were one of the most familiar trades.

vignettes.text: A queue of canoes waits under the channel; a boy holds a jar to the spout and the cold water spills over his arms.
The water-seller poles along the canals calling out; a household buys a full jar for a few cacao beans.
The overseer checks the channel for leaks and orders a sluice closed: the other channel will be cleaned tomorrow.

colonial-1620.name: Aguadores of the Tacuba road
colonial-1620.note: Water-carriers with jars on tumplines fill up at the end of the aqueduct and at the city's fountains, selling door to door.

spots.name: Fishers' and fowlers' landing
spots.summary: Where the first Mexica beached their canoes with the lake's harvest: fish, frogs, waterbirds caught in nets, insect eggs and the edible algae tecuitlatl.
details: The chronicles describe the early Mexica living on what the lake gave them: fish, axolotls, frogs, shrimps, ducks netted in flocks, and spirulina skimmed from the water and dried into cakes. They traded these, with reeds and mats, to the mainland towns for stone, wood and maize to build their city.

vignettes.text: Mist on the water. Men stretch long nets between poles across a channel in the reeds where the ducks will rise at dawn.
Women skim green scum from the shallows with fine nets and spread it on the sand to dry into cakes of tecuitlatl.
Canoes come back low in the water with fish and birds; part goes to Azcapotzalco as tribute to the Tepanec lords.

itzcoatl-1440.note: Still a busy landing, though now the island's fishermen sell to a city of tens of thousands.

spots.name: The first market of Tlatelolco
spots.summary: Tlatelolco's name means 'place of the sand mound'; from its first years its people traded the lake's produce here with merchants from the shore.
details: Tlatelolco was settled by a group of Mexica who split from Tenochtitlan, traditionally in 1337. Its people, under the protection of Azcapotzalco, specialised in trade from the start, and its market grew into the greatest in the valley.

vignettes.text: Canoes from the western shore unload firewood, stone and maize on the sand; the islanders lay out fish, birds and reed mats.
Barter is slow and loud: a basket of dried fish for a load of wood, a mat for a bag of maize.
The mainlanders push off before the evening wind; the sand is littered with fish scales and reed ends.

spots.name: An obraje (textile workshop)
spots.summary: A Spanish-owned woollen workshop where Indian, African and mixed-race workers, many of them debtors or convicts, spun, wove and dyed cloth behind locked doors.
details: Obrajes produced cheap woollens for the colonial market. Workers were often bound by debt or sentenced to work there, and were locked in; viceroys issued ordinances against abuses. Thomas Gage describes owners who lured Indians in and kept them for years. Most large obrajes were at Coyoacán and other towns, but there were some in the city.

vignettes.text: The doors are unlocked and the workers file into the long room of looms; the vats of indigo and cochineal steam in the yard.
Carders and spinners sit in rows; a foreman with a whip walks between them counting the skeins.
The doors are barred again. A worker who owes the owner for his food and clothes will not leave this year.

spots.name: School of San José de los Naturales
spots.summary: The school founded by the Flemish Franciscan Pedro de Gante in the 1520s beside San Francisco, where Indian boys learned to read, write, sing, paint and practise European crafts.
details: Pedro de Gante, said to be a relative of Charles V, taught here for half a century until his death in 1572; it is said to have had about 1,000 pupils at its height. Its open chapel held huge congregations of Indians. Painters, sculptors, musicians and craftsmen trained here decorated the churches of New Spain.

vignettes.text: Boys in white cotton chant the catechism in Nahuatl in the open chapel, a friar beating time with a rod.
In the workshops pupils grind pigments for an altarpiece and copy saints from Flemish prints.
The choir rehearses a polyphonic Mass with shawms and sackbuts for Sunday.

spots.name: Royal and Pontifical University
spots.summary: The university of Mexico, founded by royal decree in 1551, which by the 1590s had its own building on the Plaza del Volador, south of the viceregal palace.
details: Teaching began in 1553 with chairs of theology, canon and civil law, arts and rhetoric; Cervantes de Salazar gave the first lectures. Students in gowns crowded the lecture halls; degrees were conferred with processions and bullfights. Indian languages were taught from the 1580s.

vignettes.text: Students in black gowns and square caps wait for the doctor of canon law, arguing in Latin and in Spanish.
Across the square, Indian vendors on the Volador sell fruit and tamales to the students between lectures.
A new doctor rides out in procession, with trumpets, to receive his degree tomorrow in the cathedral.

spots.name: Hospital de Jesús
spots.summary: The hospital founded by Cortés in the 1520s near the place where, by tradition, he first met Moctezuma; it is still a hospital, and Cortés's bones lie in its church.
details: Cortés endowed the Hospital of the Immaculate Conception, later called de Jesús, from his estates. Its stone patios with arcades are among the oldest buildings of the city. Tradition places his meeting with Moctezuma here, at Huitzillan, where the southern causeway reached the city; some historians put it farther south, near Xoloc.

vignettes.text: Brothers carry the night's dead out through the back door; in the arcaded patio the first patients sit in the sun.
A physician from the university bleeds a merchant with a fever; the apothecary grinds herbs, some European, some Mexican.
Lamps along the arcades; the chaplain says the evening prayers in the ward.

spots.name: Market of San Juan
spots.summary: The Indian market of the barrio of San Juan Tenochtitlan, where food, pottery, herbs and charcoal were sold in the old way, on mats under awnings.
details: After the conquest the Indian parcialidad of San Juan kept its own market, one of the city's three or four great tianguis with the Plaza Mayor and Tlatelolco. Sellers paid fees to the Indian cabildo. Cacao beans still served as small change in the 17th century.

vignettes.text: Women from the chinampas lay out squash, tomatoes and greens on mats; a canoe brings charcoal to the market's edge.
A Spanish housewife's African servant haggles in Nahuatl over a basket of fish, paying in cacao beans and half-reales.
The awnings come down. The market's Indian alcalde collects the fees for the cabildo of San Juan.

spots.name: Silversmiths of the Calle de San Francisco
spots.summary: The street of the silversmiths (later Plateros), between the Plaza Mayor and San Francisco, the richest shopping street of the richest city of the Indies.
details: Silver from Zacatecas and Taxco flowed through Mexico City. Gage describes the street of the goldsmiths with its shops full of plate and jewels, and coaches of the rich parading in the Alameda; Balbuena's Grandeza mexicana (1604) praises the city's wealth. Silversmiths were licensed and their work assayed and stamped.

vignettes.text: Shutters open on rows of silver basins, candlesticks and chains; an apprentice polishes a chalice for a convent.
A coach stops; a lady and her servants examine a pearl necklace from the Pacific, brought on the Manila galleon.
The assayer's stamp is locked away; the night watch passes with a lantern.

events.title: The eagle on the cactus
events.text: Led by their god Huitzilopochtli, the wandering Mexica find on a rocky islet an eagle perched on a prickly pear cactus, the sign that they have reached their promised land. They raise a shrine of reeds and mud on the spot. The image, painted on the first page of the Codex Mendoza, is today on Mexico's flag.

events.title: Tlatelolco founded
events.text: A group of Mexica, quarrelling with the others over land, settles the sandy islet just to the north and founds Tlatelolco with its own temple and, later, its own ruler under the protection of Azcapotzalco. The twin cities will be rivals for 136 years.

events.title: The Triple Alliance overthrows Azcapotzalco
events.text: Itzcoatl of Tenochtitlan, Nezahualcoyotl of Texcoco and the ruler of Tlacopan defeat the Tepanecs of Azcapotzalco after a long war. The tributaries become an empire. Itzcoatl and his adviser Tlacaelel are said to have burned the old painted histories and written a new one centred on the Mexica.

events.title: The flood and the great dike
events.text: Heavy rains raise the lake and flood the city's streets and chinampas. Moctezuma I asks Nezahualcoyotl of Texcoco for help; the poet-king designs a dike across the lake, and workers from the allied cities drive stakes and pile stone for some 16 km. Famine years follow in the early 1450s.

events.title: Tenochtitlan conquers Tlatelolco
events.text: After years of insults between the twin cities, Axayacatl attacks Tlatelolco. Its ruler Moquihuix is thrown, or throws himself, from the top of his temple. Tlatelolco loses its ruler and is governed by military officers from Tenochtitlan, though its market and merchants go on.

events.title: Rededication of the Templo Mayor
events.text: Ahuitzotl inaugurates the enlarged temple with four days of sacrifices of captives from his wars. The chronicles claim 20,000 or even 80,400 victims; modern historians think these numbers are much exaggerated, but it was one of the greatest ceremonies the city ever saw.

events.title: Ahuitzotl's aqueduct floods the city
events.text: Ahuitzotl brings the spring of Acuecuexco from Coyoacán by a new aqueduct against the advice of its ruler. The water comes too fast: the lake rises and floods the city and its chinampas. Ahuitzotl is said to have struck his head escaping from his flooded palace. The city is rebuilt higher.

events.title: Moctezuma meets Cortés
events.text: Moctezuma, carried in a litter under a canopy of green feathers, comes out along the Iztapalapa causeway to meet Cortés and some 400 Spaniards with thousands of Tlaxcalan allies. He gives Cortés necklaces of shell and gold, then lodges them in his father's palace. Bernal Díaz: 'it was like the enchantments in the book of Amadís'.

events.title: The massacre at the feast of Toxcatl
events.text: With Cortés away fighting Narváez, Pedro de Alvarado and his men close the gates of the Sacred Precinct during the dance of the feast of Toxcatl and kill the unarmed dancers and nobles. The city rises; the Spaniards are besieged in Axayacatl's palace.

events.title: La Noche Triste
events.text: Moctezuma dead, the Spaniards try to slip out along the Tlacopan causeway in rain at night carrying their portable bridge. A woman fetching water raises the alarm. Canoes swarm round the causeway; at the Toltec canal the gap fills with drowned men and horses weighed down with gold. Several hundred Spaniards and thousands of allies die.

events.title: The fall of Tenochtitlan
events.text: After almost three months of siege by brigantines on the lake and tens of thousands of indigenous allies, with the aqueduct cut and the city already ravaged by smallpox, the last defenders hold out in Tlatelolco round the market. Cuauhtémoc is captured in a canoe trying to escape. 'Broken spears lie in the roads', says a Nahua lament written a few years later.

events.title: The Colegio de Santa Cruz opens
events.text: The viceroy Antonio de Mendoza and bishop Zumárraga open a college at Tlatelolco for sons of the Nahua nobility, taught Latin and philosophy by Franciscans. Within a generation its graduates write Latin better than many Spaniards, and help Sahagún compile the Florentine Codex.

events.title: The new cathedral is begun
events.text: Work starts on the new cathedral designed by Claudio de Arciniega, on a foundation of thousands of wooden piles and a platform of stone driven into the soft lake bed. It will take 240 years to finish and is still sinking unevenly today.

events.title: The drain of Huehuetoca
events.text: After the flood of 1604 the viceroy Luis de Velasco orders a drain to take the lakes' water out of the closed valley to the north. Under Enrico Martínez, thousands of Indian labourers dig a tunnel about 6 km long at Nochistongo near Huehuetoca in under a year. It soon caves in and silts up.

events.title: The riot against the viceroy
events.text: In a quarrel between the viceroy Gelves and the archbishop, who has excommunicated him, a crowd of Indians, mestizos, Africans and poor Spaniards storms the viceregal palace, sets it on fire and forces the viceroy to flee in disguise to San Francisco. The Crown replaces him.

events.title: The great flood
events.text: After a night of torrential rain on St Matthew's day, with the drain of Huehuetoca blocked, the lake pours into the city. The streets lie under up to two metres of water for five years; people move about by canoe, Mass is said on balconies, and thousands die or leave. There is talk of moving the capital.

stories.title: The first days of Cortés in Tenochtitlan
stories.summary: Follow the Spaniards from the meeting with Moctezuma on the southern causeway to the summits of the two great temples, as Bernal Díaz remembered it decades later.

steps.title: The meeting
steps.text: Past the fort of Xoloc, where the causeway reaches the city, Moctezuma steps down from his litter onto cloths spread by his lords. Cortés tries to embrace him and is held back: no one touches the ruler. They exchange necklaces.

steps.title: Lodged in a palace
steps.text: Moctezuma leads them to his father's palace and seats Cortés on a dais. The Spaniards fire their cannon in salute, and the city hears it with fear. Days later they find the sealed treasure room.

steps.title: The house of birds
steps.text: Bernal Díaz describes the ruler's aviary: birds from eagles to tiny hummingbirds, pools for waterbirds, and a house of jaguars, pumas and rattlesnakes 'that make a sound like bells'.

steps.title: The great market
steps.text: The Spaniards ride to Tlatelolco. They are 'astounded at the number of people and the quantity of merchandise', from gold dust in quills to slaves on poles to human excrement sold for tanning salt.

steps.title: The view from the top
steps.text: Moctezuma takes Cortés up the temple, 114 steps by Bernal's count. From the top they see the three causeways, the aqueduct from Chapultepec, the bridges and the lake 'crowded with canoes', and the white towers of temples in every town.

steps.title: The shrines
steps.text: At the Templo Mayor Cortés asks to see the gods. The shrine of Huitzilopochtli is dark, its walls black with crusted blood. Cortés suggests setting up a cross; Moctezuma, offended, stays behind to pray.

stories.title: A morning in viceregal Mexico
stories.summary: Walk through the Spanish city of the 1620s with the English friar Thomas Gage, who called it one of the richest cities in the world, built on the water.

steps.title: The Plaza Mayor
steps.text: Indian women sell fruit, tortillas and flowers under mat awnings; Spanish merchants open their shops under the arcades. Canoes unload at the Acequia Real on the square's south side.

steps.title: The viceroy's palace
steps.text: Guards at the gate, petitioners in the courts, the mint striking silver reales. In January 1624 a mob burned its doors and the viceroy fled; Gage arrived a year later and heard the story.

steps.title: Two cathedrals
steps.text: Mass in the old cathedral, low and timber-roofed, while behind it the walls of the new one rise on their raft of piles. Old stones of the Aztec temples lie in the foundations.

steps.title: The silversmiths' street
steps.text: Gage was amazed by the wealth on show in the goldsmiths' and silversmiths' shops: plate, chains, pearls and jewels, and coaches of the rich passing in the street.

steps.title: San Francisco
steps.text: The great Franciscan convent, where the friars teach Indian boys in the school of San José and the viceroy Gelves hid from the rioters.

steps.title: The Roldán landing
steps.text: Back along the Acequia, canoes from Chalco unload maize and flowers. Gage saw a city built on the lake's edge; in 1629, a few years after his visit, it drowned.
